young.html: Aristotle's Metaphysics begins with a sentence many people know: “All men by nature desire to know.” He means everyone, and he says you can tell because we enjoy our senses, especially seeing, even when we don't need them for anything.

Aristotle loved asking why. He said there are four different answers to “why is this thing the way it is?” Take a wooden table. What is it made of? Wood. What shape or plan makes it a table? A flat top on legs. Who or what made it? A carpenter. What is it for? Eating and working at. Aristotle called these the four causes.
He also noticed that things can become what they are not yet. An acorn is not an oak, but it can become one. He called this potential. When it has grown into an oak, it is an oak actually.

young.cap: Slide from what something can be to what it is. The readout gives its four causes.

young.html: Four-cause detective. Pick five objects around the house (a cup, a pencil, a shoe, a loaf of bread, a birthday card). For each one, answer the four questions: What is it made of? What makes it this kind of thing? Who or what made it? What is it for? Which question is hardest to answer for a living thing, like a cat?

full.html: The Metaphysics is a set of fourteen books of Aristotle's lectures on what he called first philosophy or wisdom: the study of the first causes of everything, and of being as being. The name was given later, probably by an editor in the first century BC, and means “the books after the Physics.” It has been read ever since as the start of the subject now called metaphysics.

full.text: All men by nature desire to know. An indication of this is the delight we take in our senses; for even apart from their usefulness they are loved for themselves; and above all others the sense of sight.
full.author: Aristotle
full.ed: The Works of Aristotle, vol. VIII, 2nd edition, Clarendon Press

full.html: Aristotle traces a ladder of knowing: animals have sensation and memory; humans add experience (knowing that this remedy helped Callias and Socrates), then art or skill (knowing why it helps all such patients), and finally wisdom, knowledge of first causes, sought for its own sake.

full.text: For it is owing to their wonder that men both now begin and at first began to philosophize; they wondered originally at the obvious difficulties, then advanced little by little and stated difficulties about the greater matters…
full.author: Aristotle
full.ed: The Works of Aristotle, vol. VIII, 2nd edition, Clarendon Press

full.html: Book I reviews earlier thinkers, who each saw part of the answer. Thales said the first principle was water; others said air, or fire, or four elements, or atoms; Plato added the Forms. Aristotle says that, taken together, they found the four kinds of cause his Physics describes.

full.html: In Book IV, Aristotle names the starting point of all thought, the principle of non-contradiction:

full.text: It is, that the same attribute cannot at the same time belong and not belong to the same subject and in the same respect…
full.author: Aristotle
full.ed: The Works of Aristotle, vol. VIII, 2nd edition, Clarendon Press

full.html: It cannot be proved, he says, because every proof uses it. But anyone who denies it can be refuted, if only he will say something, because to say anything definite is already to rule out its opposite.

The middle books ask what is most truly real. Aristotle's answer is substance (Greek ousia): individual things like this horse or this person, rather than qualities or quantities. A substance is matter shaped by a form, and the form is what makes it the kind of thing it is. Against Plato, Aristotle argues that forms are not separate from things: the form of a horse exists in horses.

Potentiality and actuality. Change is the passage from being something potentially to being it actually, as an acorn grows into an oak or a student becomes a doctor. Aristotle argues that actuality comes first: the acorn comes from an oak, and a learner needs a teacher who already knows.

In Book XII, Aristotle argues that the eternal motion of the heavens needs a first cause that is not itself moved, or else causes would go back for ever. This first mover is pure actuality, with no matter, and its life is thinking. It causes motion not by pushing but by being desired, as a goal draws us toward it:

full.text: The final cause, then, produces motion as being loved, but all other things move by being moved.
full.author: Aristotle
full.ed: The Works of Aristotle, vol. VIII, 2nd edition, Clarendon Press

full.html: Aristotle calls this first mover god, and says its thinking is “a thinking on thinking.” This is Aristotle's philosophical argument and his own view of the divine, which differs in important ways from the God of the later Jewish, Christian and Muslim thinkers who studied it.
Expecting a smooth textbook. The Metaphysics is a collection of lectures, sometimes repeating itself, with puzzles left open. Readers usually begin with Books I, IV and XII.

deep.html: The Metaphysics was studied by Arabic philosophers such as Avicenna and Averroes (who wrote so many commentaries that medieval Europe called him simply “the Commentator”), by the Jewish philosopher Maimonides, and by Christian scholars like Thomas Aquinas, later on this ladder, who used the unmoved mover argument as one of his five ways. Each read it in light of his own faith, and they disagreed with Aristotle on some points, such as whether the world had a beginning.

Early modern scientists, Galileo and Descartes among them, rejected final causes in physics, preferring to explain motion by matter and force alone. Biologists still ask “what is it for?” about organs and behaviors, and philosophers still argue over substance, essence and the principle of non-contradiction.

items: Is it true that everyone wants to know? What do you most want to know?
Does everything have a purpose? What about a mountain, or a rainstorm?
Can something be true and false at the same time, in the same way? Try to find an example, and see what goes wrong.

questions: What are you most curious about right now? Why do you think people want to know things?
Choose something you made. What were its four causes?
What is something you have the potential to become? What would help you get there?
Aristotle says a teacher must already know what a student is learning. Is that always true?
Is a rainbow made for anything? Is a heart? What's the difference?
